The Senate voted 77-15 for the bill at the beginning of June. Two-thirds of the $300 billion in spending for the farm bill will go for nutrition programs such as food stamps. Another $40 billion will go toward farm subsidies, and $30 billion is allocated for payments to farms to keep land idle and other environmental programs. **WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Congress voted overwhelmingly on Wednesday to override President George W. Bush’s veto of a $300 billion farm bill for a second time—a procedural step rendered necessary by a previous clerical error. 

The Senate approved the measure by an 80–14 vote following a 317–109 vote in the House of Representatives. Both tallies comfortably exceeded the two-thirds supermajority required to override the presidential veto issued earlier Wednesday morning.

The unusual second override stems from an error during last month’s initial override, when lawmakers discovered that 34 pages—specifically Title III of the legislation—were missing from the official document transmitted to the White House. The omission prompted concerns among House Republicans regarding the constitutional validity of the vote. The House approved the restored bill 306–110 in late May, followed by a 77–15 vote in the Senate in early June.

In rejecting the latest version, President Bush criticized Congress for failing to modify "certain objectionable, onerous and fiscally imprudent provisions," stating, "I am returning this bill for the same reasons as stated in my veto message." The President argued that the legislation maintains subsidies for wealthy agricultural producers, expands farm spending by more than $20 billion through budget gimmicks, and undermines efforts to broaden international market access for American farmers.

However, Senate Budget Committee Chairman Kent Conrad contested the administration's assessment, asserting that the legislation actually reduces government spending by $110 million. "This bill does not add to the deficit or debt, because this bill is paid for," Conrad stated. "That is not my claim. That is the finding of the Congressional Budget Office."

Under the $300 billion package, two-thirds of the funding is allocated to domestic nutrition assistance, including food stamps. An additional $40 billion is designated for direct farm subsidies, while $30 billion is earmarked for land conservation incentives and environmental programs.

**From Clerical Error to Historic Consensus: The Story of the 2008 Farm Bill**

In the late spring of 2008, the United States Capitol became the stage for an extraordinary legislative drama. What began as a standard, albeit fiercely contested, policy debate over agricultural policy turned into a historical procedural anomaly involving missing paperwork, constitutional technicalities, and an extremely rare double presidential veto override. 

At the center of the storm was the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008—commonly known as the 2008 Farm Bill. Valued at approximately $300 billion over five years, the monumental piece of legislation was designed to shape American agricultural policy, food assistance programs, and land management. However, its path to becoming law proved to be one of the most unusual in modern congressional history.

### The Initial Clash and Veto

The bill faced strong opposition from President George W. Bush. The White House argued that the legislation was fiscally irresponsible, claiming it offered excessively generous subsidies to wealthy commercial farmers at a time when crop prices were reaching record highs. Despite the administration's vocal objections, the bill enjoyed deep, broad-based bipartisan support on Capitol Hill, particularly from lawmakers representing rural districts and urban communities reliant on federal nutrition programs.

Congress initially passed the bill in mid-May 2008. As promised, President Bush exercised his constitutional authority and vetoed the measure. Congress responded swiftly: on May 21, both the House of Representatives and the Senate mustered the necessary two-thirds majorities to override the president’s veto, ostensibly enacting the bill into law.

### The 34-Page Blunder

Just as lawmakers were celebrating the legislative victory, a glaring administrative error came to light. Due to a bureaucratic oversight in the enrolling process, 34 pages of the 673-page bill had been inadvertently omitted from the official version sent to the White House for the president’s signature. 

The missing section was not trivial; it contained Title III of the bill, which governed vital foreign food aid and international agricultural trade programs. Because President Bush had vetoed—and Congress had subsequently overridden—an incomplete text, legal scholars and officials agreed that the constitutionality of the law was compromised. The foreign aid provisions were effectively in legal limbo, and the integrity of the entire legislation was threatened.

### The Unprecedented "Double Override"

To eliminate any legal ambiguity, congressional leaders realized they could not simply pass a patch for the missing pages. Instead, they were forced to re-pass the entire, unabridged $300 billion legislation through both chambers. 

Unmoved by the procedural mix-up, President Bush maintained his principled opposition to the bill's substance. When the complete version reached his desk in June, he vetoed it a second time. 

Undeterred, Congress mounted a second override effort. Demonstrating a level of bipartisan unity rarely seen in contemporary politics, lawmakers systematically dismantled the president's veto for a second time. On June 18, 2008, the House voted 317–101 and the Senate voted 80–14 to override the second veto. With these overwhelming, veto-proof majorities, the complete Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008 was officially enacted into law once and for all.

### Key Policy Deliverables and Fiscal Impact

The final enactment of the bill secured vital funding across several major sectors:

* **Nutrition Assistance:** Roughly two-thirds of the bill’s funding—over $190 billion—was dedicated to domestic food assistance programs. It expanded eligibility and increased benefits for the Food Stamp Program (renamed the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP) to help millions of low-income families cope with rising food prices.
* **Farm Safety Nets and Subsidies:** The law maintained essential traditional crop insurance and direct payments for American farmers, while also introducing a new revenue-based safety net program (ACRE) to protect producers against sudden market downturns or natural disasters.
* **Conservation Programs:** Billions of dollars were allocated to environmental programs that incentivized farmers and ranchers to remove environmentally sensitive land from agricultural production, protecting wetlands, improving water quality, and preserving wildlife habitats.

Crucially, despite its massive price tag, the bill adhered to strict fiscal guidelines. According to formal assessments by the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), the legislation was fully offset by changes to tax rules and reductions in other government spending, rendering the final law budget-neutral over its lifespan without adding to the federal deficit.

### A Lasting Legacy

The saga of the 2008 Farm Bill remains a textbook example of congressional determination and procedural resilience. What could have ended in a protracted legal breakdown was instead resolved through decisive legislative action. By executing an unprecedented second veto override, Congress not only rectified a costly administrative blunder but also reaffirmed a strong, bipartisan commitment to supporting American agriculture, environmental conservation, and national food security.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — In an unprecedented parliamentary mix-up, Congress voted overwhelmingly Thursday to override President George W. Bush’s veto of the $307 billion farm bill for a second time, bringing a bizarre, paperwork-plagued saga on Capitol Hill to a final close.

The House voted 317-109 to override the president's veto, easily exceeding the required two-thirds majority. Hours later, the Senate followed suit in an 80-13 vote, officially turning the massive, five-year agricultural and food policy package into law—again.

The rare "double override" was made necessary not by a shift in political strategy, but by a costly clerical blunder that left lawmakers and White House officials red-faced.

### A 34-page missing link

The saga began last month when Congress originally passed the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008 and sent it to the White House. President Bush, who long opposed the bill as a bloated piece of legislation that showered subsidies on wealthy farmers during a period of record farm income, promptly vetoed it. 

Congress easily overrode that veto on May 21. 

However, as lawmakers were celebrating their legislative victory, congressional aides discovered a glaring error: a 34-page section of the bill—Title III, which deals with international foreign food aid—had been accidentally omitted from the official parchment copy sent to the Oval Office. 

Because President Bush had vetoed an incomplete bill, legal experts warned that the missing trade section had not actually become law, leaving the entire $307 billion package in legal limbo.

"Human error happens," said House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer, D-Maryland, seeking to downplay the embarrassment. "We are correcting that error today, and the will of the overwhelming majority of Congress will be done."

To fix the glitch, Congress had to re-pass the missing section, re-combine it with the rest of the bill, and send the *entire* package back to President Bush’s desk. 

Unmoved by the administrative headache, President Bush promptly vetoed the complete bill on Wednesday, forcing lawmakers to hold a second round of override votes on Thursday.

### White House takes aim

The White House used the administrative mishap to take a final parting shot at Capitol Hill leadership.

"At a time of high food prices, Congress passed a farm bill that fails to reform bloated subsidies," White House Press Secretary Dana Perino said in a statement. "And in their rush to pass this bad bill, Congress couldn't even manage to send the right paperwork to the White House. It is a testament to how broken the process in Washington has become."

Republican opponents of the bill also seized on the moment to criticize the democratic leadership.

"This is an embarrassment to the institution," said Rep. John Boehner, R-Ohio, the House Minority Leader. "Not only are we overriding the president to pass a bill packed with corporate welfare, but we're doing it twice because we can't even assemble a document correctly."

### Massive scope of the bill

Despite the procedural chaos, the political reality remained unchanged: support for the farm bill was so deeply entrenched across party lines that the White House stood virtually no chance of sustaining its veto.

Lawmakers from farm states, both Democrat and Republican, fiercely defended the legislation, pointing out that nearly 70 percent of the bill's funding goes toward domestic nutrition programs, including food stamps and school lunches.

"This bill is about security—food security, energy security, and economic security," said Sen. Tom Harkin, D-Iowa, chairman of the Senate Agriculture Committee. "Yes, we had a minor bump in the road with the paperwork, but today we delivered a historic victory for American agriculture and struggling families."

The new law will extend federal farm subsidies, boost funding for land conservation, expand renewable energy research, and increase funding for food assistance programs by nearly $10 billion over the next decade.

With Thursday's Senate vote, the bill becomes law in its entirety, officially bringing an end to one of the stranger legislative episodes in recent congressional history.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — In a rare and decisive display of bipartisan unity, Congress handed President George W. Bush a stinging legislative defeat by overwhelmingly overriding his veto of the nearly $300 billion Farm Bill. 

The political victory for congressional leaders, however, was briefly overshadowed by a surreal legislative blunder: a 34-page clerical error on Capitol Hill that forced lawmakers to vote on overriding the president twice.

The legislation—the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008—defines U.S. agricultural and food policy for the next five years. Despite intense lobbying from the White House, lawmakers in both parties overwhelmingly rejected the president’s argument that the bill was financially irresponsible during a time of record farm income.

### A Bizarre Clerical Blunder

The historic override took a bizarre turn when congressional staffers discovered that an administrative oversight had occurred before the bill was sent to the White House. The official parchment copy delivered to President Bush was missing Title XV—a 34-page section containing trade and tax provisions. 

Because President Bush had vetoed an incomplete version of the bill, legal scholars warned that Title XV had not legally become law despite the initial override votes.

To remedy the mistake, Congress was forced to re-pass the complete, intact legislation under a new bill number (H.R. 6124). President Bush promptly vetoed the full package a second time, triggering a second set of override votes to permanently secure the law.

### Landslide Majorities in Both Chambers

Despite the procedural hiccup, the veto overrides highlighted the strong veto-proof majorities the bill enjoyed across party lines, particularly among lawmakers representing agricultural states.

On the initial vote, the House voted **316 to 108** to override the president, well exceeding the two-thirds majority required by the Constitution. The Senate followed suit shortly after with an **82 to 13** vote. 

When the 34-page clerical error required a second override vote on the complete bill, the results were virtually identical: the House voted **317 to 109**, and the Senate sealed the bill into law with an **80 to 14** tally.

### Bush’s Objections: "Bloated" and Unnecessary

In his veto message to Congress, President Bush sharply criticized the bill as wasteful and fiscally irresponsible, arguing that it sent government subsidies to wealthy farm conglomerates at a time when net farm income was reaching record highs.

"At a time when net farm income is projected to hit a record $92 billion this year, American taxpayers should not be asked to subsidize farmers with high incomes," Bush wrote. 

The White House specifically objected to:
* **Generous Income Caps:** Allowing married couples with non-farm adjusted gross incomes of up to $1.5 million (and farm incomes up to $1.5 million) to remain eligible for direct farm payments.
* **Cost:** Exceeding target budget baselines during a period of tight federal deficits.
* **Trade Impact:** Continuing price supports that the administration argued distorted global market prices and threatened international trade negotiations.

### Conrad Counters with CBO Data

Senate Budget Committee Chairman Kent Conrad (D-N.D.), one of the bill’s chief architects, launched a vigorous defense against the White House’s characterization of the package. 

Armed with official figures from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Conrad countered that the White House was misrepresenting the true nature of the bill's spending. He stressed that the vast majority of the funding was directed toward low-income food assistance, not wealthy commercial farmers.

"If you listen to the administration, you would think this is all farm subsidies," Conrad argued on the Senate floor, citing CBO data. "The reality is that nearly three-quarters of this bill goes to nutrition, helping lower-income Americans put food on the table during tough economic times. In fact, commodity spending for traditional farm programs is actually cut compared to previous baselines."

### Where the $300 Billion Goes

According to CBO projections, the five-year, ~$289 billion to $307 billion package allocates funding across four primary pillars:

* **Nutrition Assistance (~73% / ~$209 Billion):** The largest portion of the budget funds domestic food assistance programs, including the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP, formerly Food Stamps), school lunch programs, and emergency food bank support.
* **Commodity Programs (~11% / ~$35 Billion):** Direct payments, counter-cyclical payments, and price support loans for farmers growing major crops such as corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton, and rice.
* **Conservation (~9% / ~$25 Billion):** Programs that pay farmers and landowners to implement environmental practices, protect wetlands, and remove environmentally sensitive land from crop production (e.g., the Conservation Reserve Program and EQIP).
* **Crop Insurance (~8% / ~$22 Billion):** Federal subsidies to help farmers purchase yield and revenue protection insurance against natural disasters and market price collapses.

The remainder of the bill funds energy initiatives—including cellulosic biofuel incentives—along with forestry, horticulture, and international food aid programs.

With the second override complete, the entirety of the 2008 Farm Bill now enters into law, ending a contentious legislative battle that spanned nearly two years.

*CNN Capitol Hill producer Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.*

"It is an embarrassing mistake, to say the least," admitted one senior Democratic aide. 

To fix the procedural trainwreck, Congress was forced to execute a complex legislative maneuver: 
1. The House and Senate voted to override the veto on the 14-title version to ensure the bulk of the law took effect immediately.
2. Congress then re-passed the *entire* 15-title bill (including Title III) under a new bill number.
3. Lawmakers sent the complete version to the White House, fully prepared to override President Bush a *second* time once he inevitably vetoes it again.

Despite the White House mocking the procedural mess—with White House Press Secretary Dana Perino calling it "a mistake of legislative drafting that is quite extraordinary"—the administration could not stop the momentum of a veto-proof majority.

---

### The Budget Breakdown: Nutrition vs. Subsidies

President Bush centered his opposition to the $300 billion package on fiscal responsibility, arguing that the bill was stuffed with unnecessary subsidies for wealthy commercial farmers at a time when global commodity prices and farm incomes were reaching record highs.

"At a time of high food prices and record farm income, this bill fails to make necessary reforms," Bush wrote in his veto message. "Instead, it increases spending and continues taxpayer subsidies for wealthy individuals."

However, a closer look at the budget numbers reveals that the "farm bill" is, in reality, predominantly a massive domestic food assistance program.

According to figures from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), the $300 billion authorization breaks down as follows over five years:

*   **Nutrition Programs (67% / ~$289 Billion):** The vast majority of the bill’s funding is dedicated to domestic nutrition. This includes the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP, formerly known as Food Stamps), emergency food assistance, and school lunch programs. Expanding these benefits was a non-negotiable priority for urban Democrats facing rising food inflation nationwide.
*   **Farm Commodity Subsidies (14% / ~$42 Billion):** Direct payments, counter-cyclical payments, and price supports for traditional row crops—such as corn, wheat, soybeans, cotton, and rice. While Congress did lower the income eligibility cap for farmers receiving subsidies, Bush argued the reform was toothless, noting that couples making up to $1.5 million in farm income would still qualify.
*   **Conservation Programs (9% / ~$25 Billion):** Land-retirement programs (like the Conservation Reserve Program) and financial incentives for environmental stewardship on working farm lands.
*   **Crop Insurance (8% / ~$22 Billion):** Subsidized federal insurance to protect farmers against weather disasters and sudden market crashes.

By combining urban food stamp expansion with rural farm subsidies, the coalition behind the bill proved invincible, locking in votes from city Democrats and farm-state Republicans alike.

---

### A Weakened White House: Bush’s Veto History

The override marks a historic low point for President Bush’s legislative influence in the final year of his presidency.

For the first six years of his administration, with a Republican-controlled Congress, Bush maintained unprecedented executive discipline. He did not issue a single veto during his entire first term—a feat not accomplished since Thomas Jefferson. His first veto did not come until July 2006, when he struck down a bill expanding federal funding for stem cell research.

However, since Democrats took control of Capitol Hill in 2007, the dynamic has shifted dramatically.

Thursday’s vote marks only the **second time** President Bush’s veto has been overridden by Congress out of 11 total vetoes. The first instance occurred in November 2007, when Congress overturned his veto of the $23 billion Water Resources Development Act.

What makes the Farm Bill override particularly damaging to the White House is the sheer scale of the Republican defection. More than half of House Republicans and over two-thirds of Senate Republicans broke ranks with their president, siding with their rural constituents over the White House's fiscal doctrine. 

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-KY) and House Agriculture Committee Ranking Member Bob Goodlatte (R-VA) were among the high-profile Republicans who voted against the president.

### Looking Ahead

With the procedural snafu nearly resolved, the 2008 Farm Bill now becomes law, securing safety-net spending for low-income Americans and guaranteeing income support for American agriculture through 2012. For the Bush administration, the defeat serves as a stark reminder that as the 2008 presidential election approaches, Congress has increasingly moved on—leaving the White House struggling to hold the line on fiscal policy.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a news story about Congress overriding a Bush veto after missing pages forced a second vote on the farm bill.
counterfactuals.output:
**CAPITOL HILL** — In a rare display of bipartisan defiance—compounded by an embarrassing bureaucratic blunder—Congress voted overwhelmingly to override President George W. Bush’s veto of the $289 billion farm bill, concluding a chaotic legislative saga that required lawmakers to vote on the same override twice.

The House of Representatives voted 317 to 109 to override the executive veto, followed hours later by an 80-to-13 vote in the Senate. The veto override officially enacts the massive, five-year measure into law, dictating U.S. agricultural, food stamp, and conservation policy despite fierce opposition from the White House.

However, the final victory was delayed by a bizarre clerical error that turned high-stakes constitutional drama into a parliamentary do-over. 

Last month, Congress thought it had successfully enacted the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008 over President Bush’s veto. But just as lawmakers were celebrating, White House and congressional aides discovered that a legislative clerk had accidentally omitted an entire 34-page section of the bill—Title III, which governs foreign food aid and trade—from the official document sent to the President for his signature.

Because President Bush had vetoed a bill that was legally incomplete, constitutional lawyers warned that Congress's initial override vote was invalid. The White House had technically vetoed a document that was not the actual law passed by the House and Senate.

The oversight forced Congressional leadership into an awkward maneuver: they had to re-pass the entire 673-page bill—missing pages included—send it back to the White House, wait for President Bush to veto it a second time, and then marshal the necessary two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override him all over again.

"It was an unfortunate clerical error, but the intent of Congress has never been clearer," said a senior House leadership aide. "We were prepared to vote as many times as necessary to get this bill passed."

President Bush remained unswayed by the legislative do-over. Upon receiving the complete version of the bill, he promptly issued his second veto, repeating his criticisms that the legislation was overly expensive, bloated with subsidies for wealthy farmers at a time of record farm income, and filled with fiscal gimmicks.

"At a time of high food prices, the American people expect their government to act responsibly," the White House said in a statement accompanying the second veto. "This bill continues subsidies for higher-income farmers and increases spending by tens of billions of dollars."

Yet Bush’s veto messages found little traction on Capitol Hill, where the farm bill united an unlikely coalition of rural Republicans defending farm subsidies and urban Democrats protecting a massive expansion of the federal food stamp program (SNAP). 

Lawmakers from both parties expressed frustration at the delay caused by the lost paperwork, but rushed to put the matter to rest. 

"The American people have waited long enough for a farm bill that provides vital nutrition aid and supports our nation's producers," said House Agriculture Committee Chairman Collin Peterson (D-Minn.). "A missing stack of papers was not going to stop us from delivering for the American public."

The double-override marks a bitter defeat for the White House and a historic moment for the 110th Congress. Veto overrides are exceedingly rare in modern American politics; enacting a law over a president’s veto twice in a matter of weeks, due to a paper-shuffling glitch, is virtually unprecedented. 

With the final Senate vote in the record books, the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008 becomes law immediately, ending a nearly two-year legislative battle—and a very long month of paperwork fixes.
